questions.prompt: Convert the polar point \((r,\theta)=(2,\pi/3)\) to Cartesian coordinates.
questions.answer: Use \(x=r\cos\theta\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\). With \(r=2\) and \(\theta=\pi/3\), \(x=2\cos(\pi/3)=2(1/2)=1\). Also \(y=2\sin(\pi/3)=2(\sqrt3/2)=\sqrt3\). Therefore the Cartesian point is \((1,\sqrt3)\).

questions.prompt: Convert the Cartesian point \((3,4)\) to polar coordinates with \(r>0\) and \(0<\theta<\pi/2\).
questions.answer: Use \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). For \((3,4)\), \(r=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5\). Also \(\tan\theta=y/x=4/3\), and the point is in the first quadrant. Therefore one polar form is \((5,\arctan(4/3))\).
The polar identity is \(x^2+y^2=r^2\). Substituting into the equation gives \(r^2=16\). Since the usual polar radius for the circle is non-negative, \(r=4\). Therefore the equation is \(r=4\).

questions.prompt: Rewrite the Cartesian equation \(y=x\) in polar coordinates.
questions.answer: Use \(x=r\cos\theta\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\). Substituting gives \(r\sin\theta=r\cos\theta\). For points away from the origin, divide by \(r\) to get \(\sin\theta=\cos\theta\), so \(\theta=\pi/4\) modulo \(\pi\). Thus the line is represented by \(\theta=\pi/4\) and \(\theta=5\pi/4\), or by one full polar line convention.

questions.prompt: State the Jacobian factor \(dA\) when changing from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates.
questions.answer: In polar coordinates, \(x=r\cos\theta\) and \(y=r\sin\theta\). The area element is multiplied by the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant, which is \(r\). Therefore \(dA=r\,dr\,d\theta\).

questions.prompt: Describe the polar bounds for the annulus \(1\le x^2+y^2\le 9\).
questions.answer: Use \(x^2+y^2=r^2\). The inequality becomes \(1\le r^2\le9\), so with \(r\ge0\), \(1\le r\le3\). The full annulus goes all the way around the origin, so \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\). Therefore the bounds are \(1\le r\le3\), \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\).

The bounds describe the quarter disk \(x\ge0\), \(y\ge0\), \(x^2+y^2\le1\). In polar coordinates this is \(0\le r\le1\) and \(0\le\theta\le\pi/2\). Since \(dA=r\,dr\,d\theta\), the converted integral is \(\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^1 f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)r\,dr\,d\theta\).

questions.prompt: For the change of variables \(u=x+y\), \(v=x-y\), solve for \(x\) and \(y\) in terms of \(u\) and \(v\).
questions.answer: Add the two equations: \(u+v=(x+y)+(x-y)=2x\), so \(x=(u+v)/2\). Subtract the second from the first: \(u-v=(x+y)-(x-y)=2y\), so \(y=(u-v)/2\). Therefore \(x=\frac{u+v}{2}\) and \(y=\frac{u-v}{2}\).

Form the derivative matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}x_u&x_v\\y_u&y_v\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\). Its determinant is \((1)(-1)-(1)(1)=-2\). The absolute Jacobian factor is \(|-2|=2\). Therefore \(\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=2\).

questions.prompt: Use polar coordinates to evaluate \(\iint_R (x^2+y^2)\,dA\), where \(R\) is the disk \(x^2+y^2\le 1\).
questions.answer: In polar coordinates, \(x^2+y^2=r^2\), \(dA=r\,dr\,d\theta\), and the unit disk is \(0\le r\le1\), \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\). The integral becomes \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 r^3\,dr\,d\theta\). The inner integral is \([r^4/4]_0^1=1/4\), so the value is \(\int_0^{2\pi}1/4\,d\theta=\pi/2\).
